title: Sod Calculator - How Much Sod Do I Need? | Free Calculator & Checklist
description: Calculate how much sod you need in rolls and pallets. Free sod calculator with pre-installation checklist and care tips. Works in sq ft and sq m.

faq.q: How many pallets of sod do I need for 1,000 sq ft?
faq.a: For 1,000 square feet, you need approximately 2 pallets of sod (assuming 500 sq ft per pallet). With 5% extra for waste and cuts, order 2.1 pallets.

faq.q: How much extra sod should I order?
faq.a: Order 5-10% extra sod to account for cuts around edges, curves, and any damaged pieces. It is better to have a few extra rolls than to come up short.

faq.q: Can I lay sod over existing grass?
faq.a: No. You must remove existing grass and vegetation before laying new sod. The sod roots need direct contact with bare soil to establish.

faq.q: How long does sod take to root?
faq.a: Sod typically begins rooting within 10-14 days under proper watering. Full root establishment takes 4-6 weeks. Avoid heavy foot traffic during this period.

faq.q: Is turf the same as sod?
faq.a: Yes, turf and sod refer to the same thing: pre-grown grass that comes in rolls or slabs. Sod is the more common term in the US, while turf is widely used in the UK and Australia.

title: Grass Seed Calculator - How Much Grass Seed Do I Need?
description: Calculate how much grass seed you need by grass type. Covers new lawns and overseeding. Free calculator with seeding checklist and tips.

faq.q: How much grass seed do I need for 1,000 sq ft?
faq.a: It depends on the grass type. Kentucky Bluegrass requires about 4 lbs per 1,000 sq ft for a new lawn, while Tall Fescue requires about 10 lbs. Use the calculator for your exact amount.

faq.q: What is the difference between new lawn and overseeding rates?
faq.a: New lawn seeding uses a higher rate to ensure full coverage on bare soil. Overseeding uses roughly half the rate since you are filling in thin spots within an existing lawn.

faq.q: Can I mix different types of grass seed?
faq.a: Yes, many commercial seed mixes combine complementary grass types. Kentucky Bluegrass mixed with Perennial Ryegrass provides quick germination and long-term durability.

faq.q: When is the best time to plant grass seed?
faq.a: Plant cool-season grasses in early fall. Plant warm-season grasses in late spring to early summer.

title: Topsoil Calculator - How Much Topsoil Do I Need?
description: Calculate how much topsoil you need in cubic yards or bags. Free topsoil calculator for lawn preparation, sod installation, and garden beds.

faq.q: How much topsoil do I need for a new lawn?
faq.a: For laying sod, you need about 4 inches of topsoil depth. For 1,000 sq ft at 4 inches deep, you need approximately 12.3 cubic yards of topsoil.

faq.q: How deep should topsoil be for sod?
faq.a: A depth of 4 inches of quality topsoil is recommended before laying sod. This gives the sod roots enough depth to establish and access nutrients and water.

faq.q: How many bags of topsoil make a cubic yard?
faq.a: A standard bag of topsoil is 0.75 cubic feet. It takes 36 bags to equal one cubic yard (27 cubic feet). For large projects, bulk delivery is usually more cost effective than bags.

faq.q: Can I use garden soil instead of topsoil?
faq.a: Garden soil is typically enriched with compost, making it suitable for garden beds but not ideal for sod installation. Use screened topsoil for sod projects.

title: Mulch Calculator - How Much Mulch Do I Need?
description: Calculate how much mulch you need in cubic yards or bags. Free mulch calculator for garden beds, tree rings, and landscaping projects.

faq.q: How much mulch do I need for 1,000 sq ft?
faq.a: For 1,000 square feet at 3 inches deep, you need approximately 9.3 cubic yards of mulch, or about 125 bags (2 cu ft each).

faq.q: What is the ideal mulch depth?
faq.a: Apply mulch at a depth of 3-4 inches for new applications. Maintain existing mulch at 3-4 inches by topping up annually. Avoid piling mulch against tree trunks.

faq.q: How many bags of mulch equal a cubic yard?
faq.a: A standard bag of mulch is 2 cubic feet. It takes 13.5 bags to equal one cubic yard. For projects larger than 5 cubic yards, bulk delivery is more cost effective.

faq.q: Should I remove old mulch before adding new?
faq.a: You do not need to remove old mulch unless it has formed a matted layer preventing water penetration. Simply fluff the old mulch and add new on top.

title: Sod vs Seed - Which Is Right for Your Lawn?
description: Should you lay sod or plant grass seed? Compare cost, timeline, shade, and erosion factors.

faq.q: Is sod better than seed?
faq.a: Sod gives instant results and better erosion control but costs more. Seed is more economical and offers more variety choices but takes weeks to establish.

faq.q: How much more does sod cost than seed?
faq.a: Sod typically costs 5-10 times more than seed per square foot. However, sod provides an instant lawn while seed requires months of care before the lawn is usable.

faq.q: Can I mix sod and seed in the same yard?
faq.a: Yes, you can sod high-visibility areas and seed less visible sections. This gives you instant curb appeal where it matters while saving money on larger areas.

title: Types of Grass - Complete Lawn Grass Guide | Warm & Cool Season
description: Complete guide to lawn grass types. Compare Bermuda, Zoysia, St. Augustine, Kentucky Bluegrass, Tall Fescue, and more.

faq.q: What is the easiest grass to maintain?
faq.a: Centipede grass is often called the lazy man's grass for its very low maintenance needs. Fine Fescue is the easiest cool-season grass to maintain, needing little fertilizer and tolerating shade.

faq.q: What grass stays green all year?
faq.a: In warm climates, no grass stays truly green year-round because warm-season grasses go dormant in winter. In cool climates, cool-season grasses like Kentucky Bluegrass and Tall Fescue stay green through winter but may brown in summer without irrigation.

title: Bermuda Grass - Complete Guide | Characteristics, Pros & Cons
description: Complete guide to Bermuda grass: drought-tolerant, full-sun warm-season grass. Characteristics, climate zone, coverage rates, pros and cons.

faq.q: Does Bermuda grass need full sun?
faq.a: Yes, Bermuda grass requires at least 6-8 hours of direct sunlight daily. It has very low shade tolerance and will thin out or die in shaded areas.

title: Zoysia Grass - Complete Guide | Characteristics, Pros & Cons
description: Complete guide to Zoysia grass: dense, wear-resistant warm-season grass with moderate shade tolerance. Characteristics, coverage rates, pros and cons.

faq.q: Is Zoysia better than Bermuda?
faq.a: Zoysia tolerates more shade and cold than Bermuda but establishes more slowly. Zoysia is better for transition zone yards with mixed sun; Bermuda is better for full-sun southern lawns.

title: St. Augustine Grass - Complete Guide | Characteristics, Pros & Cons
description: Complete guide to St. Augustine grass: best shade-tolerant warm-season grass. Characteristics, climate zone, coverage rates, pros and cons.

faq.q: How much shade can St. Augustine tolerate?
faq.a: St. Augustine is the most shade-tolerant warm-season grass, surviving with as little as 4-5 hours of direct or dappled sunlight per day.

title: Kentucky Bluegrass - Complete Guide | Characteristics, Pros & Cons
description: Complete guide to Kentucky Bluegrass: rich color, soft texture, self-repairing cool-season grass. Characteristics, coverage rates, pros and cons.

faq.q: How long does Kentucky Bluegrass take to germinate?
faq.a: Kentucky Bluegrass is slow to germinate, taking 14-28 days. This is why it is often mixed with faster-germinating Perennial Ryegrass in seed blends.

title: Tall Fescue - Complete Guide | Characteristics, Pros & Cons
description: Complete guide to Tall Fescue: deep-rooted, heat and drought-tolerant cool-season grass. Best for the transition zone.

faq.q: Does Tall Fescue spread to fill bare spots?
faq.a: No, Tall Fescue is a bunch-type grass that does not spread. Bare spots must be reseeded. This is its main disadvantage compared to spreading grasses like Kentucky Bluegrass.

title: Centipede Grass - Complete Guide | Low Maintenance | Pros & Cons
description: Complete guide to Centipede grass: the lazy man's grass. Low maintenance warm-season grass for acidic, sandy soils.

faq.q: Why is Centipede called the lazy man's grass?
faq.a: Centipede grass requires very little fertilizer, grows slowly (less mowing), and tolerates poor soils. Its extremely low maintenance needs earned it this nickname.

title: Bahia & Buffalo Grass Guide | Drought-Tolerant | Pros & Cons
description: Guide to Bahia and Buffalo grass: two of the toughest, most drought-tolerant warm-season grasses for low-maintenance lawns.

faq.q: Does Bahia grass make a good lawn?
faq.a: Bahia makes a durable, low-maintenance lawn for large areas and sandy soils. However, its tall seed heads and coarse texture mean it is less attractive than Bermuda or Zoysia for formal lawns.

title: Warm Season vs Cool Season Grass - What Is the Difference?
description: Learn the difference between warm-season and cool-season grasses. Find which type is right for your climate zone.

faq.q: What is the difference between warm and cool season grass?
faq.a: Warm-season grasses grow most actively in summer heat (80-95°F) and go dormant in winter. Cool-season grasses grow most actively in spring and fall (60-75°F) and may struggle in summer heat.

title: Best Grass for Shade & Sun - Complete Sunlight Guide | Shade-Tolerant & Full-Sun
description: Find the best grass for shade, full sun, and partial sun. Compare shade tolerance of St. Augustine, Fine Fescue, Zoysia, and Tall Fescue. Includes shade lawn care tips.

faq.q: What is the best grass for full shade?
faq.a: Fine Fescue (cool-season) and St. Augustine (warm-season) are the most shade-tolerant grasses. In deep shade with less than 3 hours of sun, no grass will thrive — consider ground covers instead.

faq.q: What grass handles full sun best?
faq.a: Bermuda grass is the most sun-loving grass, thriving in 8+ hours of direct sunlight. Zoysia and Kentucky Bluegrass are also excellent full-sun performers.

title: Grass Climate Zones - Which Grass Grows Where?
description: Find which grass grows in your climate zone. Complete guide to warm-season, transition, and cool-season zones with recommended grass types.

faq.q: What grass grows best in the transition zone?
faq.a: Tall Fescue and Zoysia are the most reliable grasses for the transition zone. Tall Fescue offers year-round green with summer irrigation; Zoysia offers summer performance with winter dormancy.

title: How to Lay Sod - Step-by-Step Guide for Beginners
description: Learn how to lay sod with this step-by-step guide. From soil preparation to first watering. Avoid common mistakes for a healthy lawn.
steps: Prepare the soil by removing existing vegetation and grading for drainage
Test and amend soil pH, then apply starter fertilizer
Lightly moisten the soil surface before laying
Lay the first row along the longest straight edge, staggering seams like bricks
Trim sod around curves, beds, and sprinkler heads with a utility knife
Roll the entire lawn to press roots into firm contact with soil
Water immediately and thoroughly, soaking through sod to 6 inches deep

title: How to Plant Grass Seed - Step-by-Step Guide for Beginners
description: Learn how to plant grass seed with this step-by-step guide. From soil preparation to first watering. Best timing and common mistakes.
steps: Choose the right time: early fall for cool-season, late spring for warm-season grasses
Prepare the soil by removing vegetation and loosening the top 2-3 inches
Apply starter fertilizer high in phosphorus for root development
Spread seed with a broadcast spreader using a cross-hatch pattern
Lightly rake to cover seed with 1/8 to 1/4 inch of soil
Water gently and frequently to keep the top inch of soil consistently moist

title: How to Prepare Soil for Sod - Complete Guide
description: Learn how to prepare soil for sod installation. Step-by-step guide covering vegetation removal, grading, topsoil, and final preparation.
steps: Remove all existing vegetation with non-selective herbicide, wait 10-14 days, then clear dead material
Rough grade the area, sloping away from structures at 1 inch per 4 feet
Add 4 inches of screened topsoil if existing soil is poor
Loosen the top 4-6 inches of soil to improve drainage and root penetration
Final grade and smooth the surface, removing rocks and debris
Apply starter fertilizer and lightly rake into the soil
Lightly water to moisten the surface before laying sod

title: When to Lay Sod - Best Time of Year by Climate
description: Find the best time to lay sod in your climate zone. Seasonal guide for warm-season and cool-season regions.

faq.q: Can you lay sod in the summer?
faq.a: Yes, but you must water more frequently to prevent heat stress. Install early in the morning and water immediately and deeply. In extreme heat (above 95°F), consider waiting until temperatures moderate.

faq.q: Can you lay sod in the winter?
faq.a: Sod can be laid in winter as long as the ground is not frozen. The grass will be dormant and will not root until spring, but it will not die if properly installed.

title: New Sod Care Guide - Watering, Mowing & Maintenance
description: Complete new sod care guide. Watering schedule, first mowing, fertilizing, and troubleshooting. Keep your new sod healthy.

faq.q: How often should I water new sod?
faq.a: Water daily for the first 2 weeks, keeping the soil consistently moist but not waterlogged. After 2 weeks, gradually reduce frequency while increasing depth to encourage deep root growth.

faq.q: How long before you can walk on new sod?
faq.a: Wait at least 2 weeks before light foot traffic on new sod. Keep children and pets off the lawn during this period. Full use can resume after 6 weeks.

title: Common Sod Mistakes to Avoid - Do Not Make These Errors
description: Avoid these 6 common sod mistakes: ordering wrong, laying over grass, waiting to install, watering wrong, mowing too soon, and using weed killer too early.

faq.q: What is the biggest mistake when laying sod?
faq.a: Not removing existing grass and vegetation before laying new sod. The old grass dies and rots, creating an uneven surface and preventing the new sod from rooting into the soil.

faq.q: Why is my new sod turning brown?
faq.a: Browning sod is usually caused by underwatering or poor soil contact. Check that edges are firmly pressed together and against the soil. Water deeply and ensure the sod is not lifting from the soil below.
